findings.title: `queued` default is evaluated once at import time
findings.body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` runs a single time, when the module is imported. Every `AssignmentSource` built without an explicit `queued`, including all of those from `from_integration`, gets the same timestamp: the process start time. On long-running web and worker processes that value can be hours or days stale, so `queued` never reflects when the assignment was queued. Use `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The new `test_to_dict` only checks that `queued` is not None, so it cannot catch this.

findings.title: Raw datetime passed in Celery task kwargs
findings.body: `assignment_source.to_dict()` uses `dataclasses.asdict`, so the `queued` value is a raw `datetime`. That dict is passed as `assignment_source_dict` in `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async` kwargs. Sentry expects task parameters to be JSON-safe primitives, and a datetime is not. With a JSON serializer this either fails to serialize, gets flagged as a bad-pickle parameter, or reaches the worker as a string. In the string case `from_dict` still builds the object, because dataclasses do no type checking, and `queued` silently ends up as a `str` despite its `datetime` annotation. The tests run tasks eagerly with `self.tasks()`, so the serialization round-trip is never exercised. Serialize `queued` as an ISO string or epoch int and parse it back in `from_dict`.

findings.title: Cycle suppression works per integration, so other linked issues on the same integration stop syncing
findings.body: The new check returns False whenever `sync_source.integration_id` equals the installation's integration id. A Sentry group can be linked to several external issues on the same integration, for example two Jira tickets on one Jira install. If the assignee changes on ticket A, the outbound sync to ticket B is now skipped too, because B shares A's integration. Before this change B would have been updated, so B is left with a stale assignee. The suppression should target the originating external issue (for example by carrying the external issue key or id in `AssignmentSource`) rather than every issue on that integration.

findings.title: `assignment_source` added to abstract `sync_status_outbound` but never passed or used
findings.body: The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source` parameter. No caller passes it, the status sync path never builds an `AssignmentSource`, and concrete implementations don't consume it. The signature suggests status sync cycles are also prevented, but inbound status webhooks still trigger outbound status syncs back to the same integration. Either wire it through the status path or drop the parameter so the abstract signature doesn't mislead implementers.

findings.title: `from_dict` silently returns None on any unexpected key, turning off cycle protection
findings.body: `from_dict` does `cls(**input_dict)` and swallows `TypeError`/`ValueError` by returning None. The task then calls `should_sync(..., None)`, which skips the source check and syncs back to the originating integration. This will happen if the payload ever gains a field during a mixed-version deploy, or if `queued` cannot be handled. The sync-cycle protection is lost without any log or metric. At minimum, log when parsing fails. Better, ignore unknown keys and build the object from the known fields.

findings.title: No end-to-end test that inbound sync suppresses outbound to the same integration
findings.body: The new test only calls `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` directly with a hand-built `AssignmentSource`. Nothing checks that `sync_group_assignee_inbound` actually attaches the source for both assign and deassign, which is the code path that fixes the reported loop. Nothing checks that a different integration linked to the same group still receives the outbound sync. There is also no deassign test with a matching source. The inbound tests at the end of this file don't mock or assert on `sync_assignee_outbound` at all.
